questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is environmental pollution?

options.A: Any change in the environment caused by natural events
options.B: An undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or land that harms living organisms, ecosystems, property or human well-being
options.C: The addition of beneficial substances to the environment
options.D: Only the contamination of air by harmful gases

questions.explanation: Environmental pollution is an undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or land that harms living organisms, ecosystems, property or human well-being.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is a pollutant?

options.A: Any natural substance present in the environment
options.B: A substance, organism or form of energy present in the environment at a concentration or intensity capable of causing harm
options.C: Only chemical substances released by industries
options.D: A beneficial agent that improves environmental quality

questions.explanation: A pollutant is a substance, organism or form of energy present in the environment at a concentration or intensity capable of causing harm; examples include smoke, sewage, pesticides, heavy metals, plastics and excessive sound.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is a contaminant?

options.A: A substance that is always harmful to the environment
options.B: An unwanted substance present in a medium; it is called a pollutant when its presence or level causes or is likely to cause adverse effects
options.D: A type of energy that causes pollution

questions.explanation: A contaminant is an unwanted substance present in a medium; it is called a pollutant when its presence or level causes or is likely to cause adverse effects.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Which of the following are the major forms of pollution specified in the syllabus?

options.A: Air, water, soil, noise and plastic pollution
options.B: Only air and water pollution
options.C: Thermal, radioactive and light pollution only
options.D: Air, water, soil, noise, thermal, radioactive, light and plastic pollution

questions.explanation: The syllabus specifically requires air, water, soil, noise and plastic pollution. The major forms include air, water, soil or land, noise, thermal, radioactive, light and plastic pollution.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is a point source of pollution?

options.A: Diffuse pollution arising from many scattered sources
options.B: A single identifiable source from which pollution is discharged, such as a factory chimney, sewage outlet or industrial effluent pipe
options.C: Pollution that occurs only during natural disasters

questions.explanation: A point source is a single identifiable source from which pollution is discharged, such as a factory chimney, sewage outlet or industrial effluent pipe.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is a non-point source of pollution?

options.A: A single factory chimney
options.B: A sewage outlet pipe
options.C: Diffuse pollution arising from many scattered sources, such as agricultural runoff or urban stormwater

questions.explanation: A non-point source is diffuse pollution arising from many scattered sources, such as agricultural runoff carrying fertilisers and pesticides or urban stormwater carrying oil and litter.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is biodegradable waste?

options.A: Waste that never decomposes
options.B: Waste that microorganisms can break down into simpler substances under suitable environmental conditions
options.C: Waste made only of plastic materials
options.D: Waste that causes pollution only in water

questions.explanation: Biodegradable waste is waste that microorganisms can break down into simpler substances under suitable environmental conditions; examples include food scraps, leaves and many forms of untreated paper.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is non-biodegradable waste?

options.A: Waste that decomposes quickly through natural biological processes
options.B: Waste that does not readily decompose through natural biological processes
options.D: Waste that is always harmful to humans

questions.explanation: Non-biodegradable waste does not readily decompose through natural biological processes; examples include many plastics, glass and certain synthetic chemicals.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is bioaccumulation?

options.A: The increase in concentration of a pollutant at higher trophic levels
options.B: The gradual build-up of a chemical in an organism over time because uptake exceeds elimination
options.C: The breakdown of pollutants by microorganisms
options.D: The movement of pollutants from water to air

questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation is the gradual build-up of a chemical, often a persistent pollutant, in an organism over time because uptake exceeds elimination.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is biomagnification?

options.A: The breakdown of pollutants by bacteria
options.B: The increase in concentration of a persistent pollutant at successively higher trophic levels in a food chain
options.C: The dilution of pollutants in water bodies
options.D: The absorption of nutrients by plants

questions.explanation: Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a persistent pollutant at successively higher trophic levels in a food chain; methylmercury and certain persistent organic pollutants are examples.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is eutrophication?

options.A: The depletion of nutrients in a water body
options.B: Excessive enrichment of a water body with nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, which can cause algal blooms, oxygen depletion and fish deaths
options.C: The increase in dissolved oxygen in water

questions.explanation: Eutrophication is excessive enrichment of a water body with nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, which can cause algal blooms, oxygen depletion and fish deaths.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is sustainable development?

options.A: Development that exploits all natural resources for maximum profit
options.B: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
options.C: Development that focuses only on economic growth
options.D: Development that stops all industrial activities

questions.explanation: Sustainable development is development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is the polluter pays principle?

options.A: The government pays for all pollution cleanup
options.B: The person or organisation responsible for pollution should bear the cost of preventing, controlling and remedying the environmental damage, subject to applicable law
options.C: Polluters are exempt from any liability
options.D: Only industries pay for pollution, not individuals

questions.explanation: The polluter pays principle means that the person or organisation responsible for pollution should bear the cost of preventing, controlling and remedying the environmental damage, subject to applicable law.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is the precautionary principle?

options.A: Action should be taken only after scientific certainty is established
options.B: Preventive action is required where there is a credible risk of serious or irreversible environmental harm, even if scientific certainty is incomplete
options.C: Environmental damage should be ignored until proven harmful
options.D: Development should always take precedence over environmental protection

questions.explanation: The precautionary principle requires preventive action where there is a credible risk of serious or irreversible environmental harm, even if scientific certainty is incomplete.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is carrying capacity?

options.A: The maximum amount of pollution an environment can absorb without any change
options.B: The maximum population or level of activity that an environment can sustain over time without unacceptable degradation of its natural resources and ecological functions
options.C: The total weight of pollutants in an ecosystem
options.D: The rate at which pollutants are discharged into the environment

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum population or level of activity that an environment can sustain over time without unacceptable degradation of its natural resources and ecological functions.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is air pollution?

options.A: The presence of only gases in the atmosphere
options.B: The presence of solid particles, liquid droplets or harmful gases in the atmosphere at levels that adversely affect human health, other organisms, property or the environment
options.C: The natural variation in atmospheric temperature
options.D: The presence of oxygen in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Air pollution is the presence of solid particles, liquid droplets or harmful gases in the atmosphere at levels that adversely affect human health, other organisms, property or the environment.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Which of the following are major sources of air pollution?

options.A: Motor vehicles, thermal power plants, industries, construction and demolition, road dust, mining, brick kilns, diesel generator sets, domestic fuel combustion, waste burning and forest fires
options.B: Only motor vehicles
options.C: Only thermal power plants and industries

questions.explanation: Major sources include motor vehicles, thermal power plants, industries, construction and demolition, road dust, mining, brick kilns, diesel generator sets, domestic fuel combustion, waste burning and forest fires.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are primary air pollutants?

options.A: Pollutants formed by chemical reactions in the atmosphere
options.B: Pollutants emitted directly into the atmosphere from a source

questions.explanation: Primary air pollutants are emitted directly into the atmosphere from a source; examples include carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, volatile organic compounds and lead.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are secondary air pollutants?

options.A: Pollutants emitted directly from vehicles
options.B: Pollutants formed in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving primary pollutants
options.C: Pollutants that are always less harmful than primary pollutants
options.D: Pollutants that come only from natural sources

questions.explanation: Secondary air pollutants form in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving primary pollutants; examples include ground-level ozone, some secondary particulate matter and components of photochemical smog.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is particulate matter?

options.A: Only solid dust particles in the air
options.B: A mixture of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air, including dust, soot, smoke, metals, salts and organic compounds
options.C: Only liquid droplets in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Particulate matter (PM) is a mixture of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air, including dust, soot, smoke, metals, salts and organic compounds.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is PM10?

options.A: Particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 micrometres or less that can enter the respiratory tract
options.B: Particles with a diameter of exactly 10 millimetres
options.C: Particles that cannot enter the human body
options.D: Gaseous pollutants with a molecular weight of 10

questions.explanation: PM10 refers to inhalable particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 micrometres or less; these particles can enter the respiratory tract.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is PM2.5?

options.A: Particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 millimetres or less
options.B: Fine particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less that can penetrate deep into the lungs and some components can enter the bloodstream
options.C: Particles that are larger than PM10
options.D: Gaseous pollutants with a molecular weight of 2.5

questions.explanation: PM2.5 refers to fine particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less; they can penetrate deep into the lungs and some components can enter the bloodstream.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Why is PM2.5 generally more dangerous than larger dust particles?

options.A: It is always more visible
options.B: It can penetrate deeper into the lungs, may carry toxic substances and is associated with cardiovascular and respiratory disease
options.C: It is heavier and settles faster
options.D: It is less harmful because it is smaller

questions.explanation: PM2.5 can penetrate deeper into the lungs, may carry toxic substances and is associated with cardiovascular and respiratory disease; risk depends on concentration, composition and exposure duration.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is carbon monoxide and how is it produced?

options.A: A colourless, odourless poisonous gas produced mainly by incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels
options.B: A green gas produced by photosynthesis
options.C: A gas produced only by volcanic eruptions
options.D: A harmless gas produced by complete combustion

questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colourless, odourless poisonous gas produced mainly by incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels, including vehicle fuel and biomass.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?

options.A: It causes acid rain directly
options.B: It binds strongly with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity
options.D: It causes eutrophication in water bodies

questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds strongly with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and potentially causing headache, dizziness, unconsciousness or death.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the major sources of sulphur dioxide?

options.A: Burning sulphur-containing coal and oil, certain industrial processes and some smelting operations
options.B: Photosynthesis by plants

questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide (SO2) is mainly released by burning sulphur-containing coal and oil, certain industrial processes and some smelting operations.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the effects of sulphur dioxide?

options.A: It only affects plants
options.B: It irritates the respiratory system, can worsen asthma and contributes to the formation of sulphate particles and acid deposition
options.C: It has no harmful effects on humans

questions.explanation: SO2 irritates the respiratory system, can worsen asthma and contributes to the formation of sulphate particles and acid deposition.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are nitrogen oxides (NOx)?

options.A: Gases produced mainly during high-temperature combustion in vehicles, power plants and industries
options.B: Gases produced only by plants
options.C: Gases found only in the upper atmosphere
options.D: Harmless gases produced by complete combustion

questions.explanation: Nitrogen oxides (NOx), particularly nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide, are produced mainly during high-temperature combustion in vehicles, power plants and industries.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the effects of nitrogen dioxide?

options.A: It only affects the ozone layer
options.B: It irritates airways, contributes to respiratory problems and participates in the formation of ground-level ozone, nitrate particles and acid deposition
options.C: It has no effect on human health

questions.explanation: Nitrogen dioxide irritates airways, contributes to respiratory problems and participates in the formation of ground-level ozone, nitrate particles and acid deposition.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is ground-level ozone?

options.A: A primary pollutant emitted directly from vehicles
options.B: A secondary pollutant formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight; it is harmful to human health and vegetation
options.C: A beneficial gas that protects the environment
options.D: A gas found only in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight; it is harmful to human health and vegetation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is photochemical smog?

options.A: A brownish urban air pollution mixture formed when sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds
options.B: Smoke from burning coal only
options.C: A natural fog that occurs in winter
options.D: A mixture of water vapour and dust

questions.explanation: Photochemical smog is a brownish urban air pollution mixture formed when sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ozone and other oxidants.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is acid rain?

options.A: Rain that contains only water
options.B: Precipitation or deposition made unusually acidic mainly by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides reacting in the atmosphere to form sulphuric and nitric acids
options.C: Rain that falls only in industrial areas
options.D: Rain with a pH greater than 7

questions.explanation: Acid rain is precipitation or deposition made unusually acidic mainly by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides reacting in the atmosphere to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?

options.A: The cooling of the Earth's surface by greenhouse gases
options.B: The warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere caused by greenhouse gases absorbing and re-emitting outgoing infrared radiation
options.C: The reflection of sunlight by the ozone layer
options.D: The absorption of ultraviolet rays by the atmosphere

questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere caused by greenhouse gases absorbing and re-emitting outgoing infrared radiation; the natural greenhouse effect makes Earth habitable, while its enhancement drives global warming.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Is air pollution the same as climate change?

options.A: Yes, they are identical
options.B: No, air pollution concerns harmful substances in the air and their effects, while climate change concerns long-term shifts in climate; some pollutants such as black carbon and methane influence both
options.C: Yes, both refer to the same atmospheric phenomena
options.D: No, air pollution has no relation to climate

questions.explanation: Air pollution concerns harmful substances in the air and their effects, while climate change concerns long-term shifts in climate; some pollutants, such as black carbon and methane, influence both.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the major health effects of air pollution?

options.A: Only respiratory problems
options.B: Asthma, bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory infections, lung cancer, heart disease, stroke and adverse pregnancy outcomes

questions.explanation: Air pollution can cause or worsen asthma, bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory infections, lung cancer, heart disease, stroke and adverse pregnancy outcomes; children, older people and people with existing illnesses are especially vulnerable.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How does air pollution affect plants and crops?

options.A: It always improves plant growth
options.B: It can damage leaf tissues, reduce photosynthesis and crop yields, deposit toxic substances on vegetation and contribute to acidification and ozone injury
options.C: It has no effect on plants

questions.explanation: Air pollution can damage leaf tissues, reduce photosynthesis and crop yields, deposit toxic substances on vegetation and contribute to acidification and ozone injury.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How does air pollution contribute to acidification?

options.A: By directly releasing acids into water bodies
options.B: Sulphur and nitrogen compounds released into the atmosphere can form acids that are deposited through rain, snow, fog or dry particles, affecting soils, lakes, forests and buildings
options.C: By increasing the pH of rainwater

questions.explanation: Sulphur and nitrogen compounds released into the atmosphere can form acids that are deposited through rain, snow, fog or dry particles, affecting soils, lakes, forests and buildings.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is an Air Quality Index (AQI)?

options.A: A direct measurement of pollutant concentration
options.B: A communication tool that converts measurements of several air pollutants into a common scale to describe air quality and associated health concern
options.C: A unit of measuring wind speed

questions.explanation: The Air Quality Index is a communication tool that converts measurements of several air pollutants into a common scale to describe air quality and associated health concern.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Which organisation publishes India's national AQI framework?

options.A: Karnataka State Pollution Control Board
options.B: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)

questions.explanation: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) developed India's National Air Quality Index framework, with air quality information made available through CPCB and associated monitoring systems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Which pollutants are included in India's AQI calculation?

options.A: Only PM10 and PM2.5
options.B: Up to eight pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone, ammonia and lead

questions.explanation: The framework uses up to eight pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone, ammonia and lead, subject to the availability of required monitoring data.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are India's National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) based on the 2009 notification for PM10?

options.A: Annual 40 μg/m³ and 24-hour 60 μg/m³
options.B: Annual 60 μg/m³ and 24-hour 100 μg/m³

questions.explanation: The annual average standard for PM10 is 60 micrograms per cubic metre and the 24-hour standard is 100 micrograms per cubic metre.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are India's NAAQS for PM2.5 under the 2009 notification?

options.A: Annual 60 μg/m³ and 24-hour 100 μg/m³
options.B: Annual 40 μg/m³ and 24-hour 60 μg/m³

questions.explanation: The annual average standard for PM2.5 is 40 micrograms per cubic metre and the 24-hour standard is 60 micrograms per cubic metre.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are India's NAAQS for sulphur dioxide under the 2009 notification?

options.A: Annual 50 μg/m³ for most areas and 20 μg/m³ for ecologically sensitive areas; 24-hour 80 μg/m³
options.B: Annual 40 μg/m³ and 24-hour 60 μg/m³

questions.explanation: The annual standard is 50 μg/m³ for most areas and 20 μg/m³ for ecologically sensitive areas; the 24-hour standard is 80 μg/m³.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are India's NAAQS for nitrogen dioxide under the 2009 notification?

options.A: Annual 50 μg/m³ and 24-hour 80 μg/m³
options.B: Annual 40 μg/m³ for most areas and 30 μg/m³ for ecologically sensitive areas; 24-hour 80 μg/m³

questions.explanation: The annual standard is 40 μg/m³ for most areas and 30 μg/m³ for ecologically sensitive areas; the 24-hour standard is 80 μg/m³.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What measures reduce vehicular air pollution?

options.A: Increasing the number of private vehicles
options.B: Reliable public transport, walking and cycling infrastructure, cleaner fuels, electric mobility, vehicle maintenance, valid pollution-under-control certification, traffic management and strict enforcement of emission standards
options.D: Encouraging older vehicles on the road

questions.explanation: Measures include reliable public transport, walking and cycling infrastructure, cleaner fuels, electric mobility, vehicle maintenance, valid pollution-under-control certification, traffic management and strict enforcement of emission standards.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How can construction-related air pollution be controlled?

options.A: By ignoring dust generation
options.B: By covering materials and trucks, preventing debris spillage, using dust screens, controlling cutting and demolition dust, storing materials properly and using water spraying or suitable dust-control equipment
options.C: By increasing construction speed without precautions
options.D: By burning construction waste on site

questions.explanation: Construction sites should cover materials and trucks, prevent debris spillage, use dust screens, control cutting and demolition dust, store materials properly, and use water spraying or suitable dust-control equipment without wasting water.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How can road-dust pollution be reduced?

options.A: By allowing soil and debris to accumulate on roads
options.B: Through mechanised or vacuum sweeping where suitable, paved shoulders, repaired roads, covered transport of construction materials, green buffers and prevention of soil and debris accumulation
options.C: By increasing vehicle speed on unpaved roads

questions.explanation: Road dust can be reduced through mechanised or vacuum sweeping where suitable, paved shoulders, repaired roads, covered transport of construction materials, green buffers and prevention of soil and debris accumulation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How can industrial air pollution be controlled?

options.A: By increasing emissions without treatment
options.B: By using cleaner fuels and processes, improving energy efficiency, installing suitable particulate and gas-control equipment such as bag filters, electrostatic precipitators and scrubbers, and continuously monitoring emissions where required
options.C: By removing all emission monitoring systems
options.D: By burning waste materials in open areas

questions.explanation: Industries can use cleaner fuels and processes, improve energy efficiency, install suitable particulate and gas-control equipment such as bag filters, electrostatic precipitators and scrubbers, and continuously monitor emissions where required.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is an electrostatic precipitator?

options.A: A device that removes fine particles from industrial exhaust by electrically charging particles and collecting them on oppositely charged plates
options.B: A device that increases particulate emissions
options.C: A device that cools industrial exhaust
options.D: A device that adds moisture to exhaust gases

questions.explanation: An electrostatic precipitator removes fine particles from industrial exhaust by electrically charging particles and collecting them on oppositely charged plates.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is a scrubber?

options.A: A device that removes selected gases or particles from an exhaust stream, commonly by bringing the gas into contact with a liquid or other treatment medium
options.B: A device that increases gas emissions
options.C: A device used only for water purification
options.D: A device that generates electricity from exhaust

questions.explanation: A scrubber is an air-pollution-control device that removes selected gases or particles from an exhaust stream, commonly by bringing the gas into contact with a liquid or other treatment medium.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)?

options.A: A state-level programme for Karnataka only
options.B: A national programme launched in 2019 to improve air quality through city action plans, monitoring, source identification, capacity building and coordinated pollution-control measures
options.C: A programme that promotes air pollution
options.D: A programme for cleaning rivers only

questions.explanation: NCAP is a national programme launched in 2019 to improve air quality through city action plans, monitoring, source identification, capacity building and coordinated pollution-control measures.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are important air-pollution concerns in Karnataka?

options.A: Only industrial emissions
options.B: Traffic and road dust in Bengaluru and other growing cities, construction and demolition dust, industrial emissions, mining and quarrying dust, diesel generator emissions, open waste burning and seasonal biomass or forest fires

questions.explanation: Important concerns include traffic and road dust in Bengaluru and other growing cities, construction and demolition dust, industrial emissions, mining and quarrying dust, diesel generator emissions, open waste burning and seasonal biomass or forest fires.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the major sources identified in Bengaluru's air-pollution studies?

options.A: Only industrial emissions
options.B: Transport emissions and resuspended road dust as major contributors, along with construction and demolition, waste burning, fuel combustion and industrial sources

questions.explanation: Studies identify transport emissions and resuspended road dust as major contributors, along with construction and demolition, waste burning, fuel combustion and industrial sources; the relative shares vary by pollutant, location and study year.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: According to the Karnataka State Clean Air Action Plan 2024, what was the prominent source of PM2.5 in the Bengaluru source-apportionment figure?

options.A: Industrial emissions at about 50%
options.B: Transportation at about 39.9%

questions.explanation: Transportation was shown as the largest listed source at about 39.9% in that study's PM2.5 source-apportionment figure; soil dust was about 25.3%. These are study-specific estimates, not universal or current daily shares.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: According to the Karnataka State Clean Air Action Plan 2024, what was the share of soil dust in Bengaluru's PM2.5 source-apportionment figure?

options.A: About 39.9%
options.B: About 25.3%

questions.explanation: Transportation was shown as the largest listed source at about 39.9% in that study's PM2.5 source-apportionment figure; soil dust was about 25.3%. These are study-specific estimates.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Which industrial area in Bengaluru has been identified in environmental assessments as requiring groundwater-contamination attention?

options.A: Whitefield Industrial Area
options.B: Peenya Industrial Area

questions.explanation: Peenya Industrial Area has been identified as an area where clusters of small electroplating and surface-treatment units can create groundwater-contamination risks if wastewater is inadequately treated.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are practical city-level measures for improving Bengaluru's air quality?

options.A: Increasing private vehicle use
options.B: Improving public transport and last-mile connectivity, controlling road and construction dust, preventing open waste burning, maintaining vehicles, shifting to cleaner transport and fuels, and enforcing industrial emission standards

questions.explanation: Priorities include improving public transport and last-mile connectivity, controlling road and construction dust, preventing open waste burning, maintaining vehicles, shifting to cleaner transport and fuels, and enforcing industrial emission standards.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is water pollution?

options.A: The addition of beneficial minerals to water
options.B: The contamination or undesirable alteration of surface water or groundwater that makes it harmful or unsuitable for drinking, domestic use, agriculture, industry or aquatic ecosystems
options.C: The natural variation in water temperature
options.D: The presence of dissolved oxygen in water

questions.explanation: Water pollution is the contamination or undesirable alteration of surface water or groundwater that makes it harmful or unsuitable for drinking, domestic use, agriculture, industry or aquatic ecosystems.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the major sources of water pollution?

options.A: Only industrial effluents
options.B: Untreated domestic sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, landfill leachate, mining waste, oil spills, detergents, plastics, thermal discharges and contaminated stormwater

questions.explanation: Major sources include untreated domestic sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, landfill leachate, mining waste, oil spills, detergents, plastics, thermal discharges and contaminated stormwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is domestic sewage?

options.A: Wastewater from industries only
options.B: Wastewater from homes and similar establishments containing human waste, food residues, soaps, detergents, pathogens and other organic and inorganic materials

questions.explanation: Domestic sewage is wastewater from homes and similar establishments containing human waste, food residues, soaps, detergents, pathogens and other organic and inorganic materials.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is industrial effluent?

options.A: Wastewater from homes
options.B: Wastewater discharged from industrial processes; its composition may include acids, alkalis, oils, dyes, solvents, organic chemicals and toxic metals

questions.explanation: Industrial effluent is wastewater discharged from industrial processes; its composition may include acids, alkalis, oils, dyes, solvents, organic chemicals and toxic metals.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How does agricultural runoff pollute water?

options.A: By adding clean water to rivers
options.B: Rain or irrigation water can carry fertilisers, pesticides, animal waste and eroded soil from agricultural land into rivers, lakes and groundwater

questions.explanation: Rain or irrigation water can carry fertilisers, pesticides, animal waste and eroded soil from agricultural land into rivers, lakes and groundwater.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)?

options.A: The amount of oxygen produced by aquatic plants
options.B: The amount of dissolved oxygen required by microorganisms to biologically decompose biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions, commonly measured as a five-day test at 20°C
options.C: The total oxygen content of water
options.D: The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen required by microorganisms to biologically decompose biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions, commonly measured as a five-day test at 20°C.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What does a high BOD value indicate?

options.A: A high load of biodegradable organic pollution and a greater potential for oxygen depletion in the receiving water body
options.B: High dissolved oxygen levels

questions.explanation: A high BOD generally indicates a high load of biodegradable organic pollution and a greater potential for oxygen depletion in the receiving water body.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD)?

options.A: The oxygen equivalent of the chemically oxidisable substances in a water sample; it is used as an indicator of the total oxidisable pollution load
options.B: The oxygen required by aquatic organisms
options.C: The oxygen produced by chemical reactions in water
options.D: The total dissolved oxygen in water

questions.explanation: COD is the oxygen equivalent of the chemically oxidisable substances in a water sample; it is used as an indicator of the total oxidisable pollution load.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is Dissolved Oxygen (DO)?

options.A: The oxygen present in water and available to aquatic organisms; low DO can stress or kill fish and other aquatic life
options.B: The oxygen in the atmosphere
options.C: The oxygen required for BOD test

questions.subject: Environmental Science

questions.question: What is the activated sludge process?

questions.subject: Environmental Science

questions.subject: Environmental Science

questions.subject: Environmental Science

questions.explanation: A scrubber is an air-pollution-control device that removes selected gases or particles from an exhaust stream, commonly by bringing the gas into contact with a liquid or other treatment medium.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is water pollution?

questions.question: What are the major sources of water pollution?

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is industrial effluent?

options.B: Wastewater discharged from industrial processes; its composition may include acids, alkalis, oils, dyes, solvents, organic chemicals and toxic metals

questions.question: How does agricultural runoff pollute water?

options.B: Rain or irrigation water can carry fertilisers, pesticides, animal waste and eroded soil from agricultural land into rivers, lakes and groundwater

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)?

options.A: The amount of oxygen produced by aquatic plants
options.B: The amount of dissolved oxygen required by microorganisms to biologically decompose biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions, commonly measured as a five-day test at 20°C
options.C: The total oxygen content of water
options.D: The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen required by microorganisms to biologically decompose biodegradable organic matter in a water sample under specified test conditions, commonly measured as a five-day test at 20°C.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What does a high BOD value indicate?

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD)?

options.A: The oxygen equivalent of the chemically oxidisable substances in a water sample; it is used as an indicator of the total oxidisable pollution load
options.B: The oxygen required by aquatic organisms
options.C: The oxygen produced by chemical reactions in water
options.D: The total dissolved oxygen in water

questions.explanation: COD is the oxygen equivalent of the chemically oxidisable substances in a water sample; it is used as an indicator of the total oxidisable pollution load.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is Dissolved Oxygen (DO)?

options.A: The oxygen present in water and available to aquatic organisms; low DO can stress or kill fish and other aquatic life
options.B: The oxygen in the atmosphere
options.C: The oxygen required for BOD test

questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen is the oxygen present in water and available to aquatic organisms; low DO can stress or kill fish and other aquatic life.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is the relationship between BOD and dissolved oxygen?

options.A: High BOD leads to high dissolved oxygen
options.B: When biodegradable organic matter enters water, microorganisms consume oxygen while decomposing it; therefore, rising BOD often leads to falling dissolved oxygen
options.C: BOD and dissolved oxygen are unrelated
options.D: Low BOD leads to low dissolved oxygen

questions.explanation: When biodegradable organic matter enters water, microorganisms consume oxygen while decomposing it; therefore, rising BOD often leads to falling dissolved oxygen.

questions.subject: Environmental Science

questions.subject: Environmental Science

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is leachate?

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How does water pollution affect aquatic ecosystems?

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is an Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP)?

options.A: A plant that treats industrial wastewater to remove or reduce pollutants before reuse or lawful discharge
options.B: A plant that treats domestic sewage only
options.D: A plant that produces drinking water from seawater

questions.explanation: An ETP treats industrial wastewater to remove or reduce pollutants before reuse or lawful discharge.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is a Sewage Treatment Plant (STP)?

options.A: A plant that treats industrial wastewater only
options.B: A plant that treats domestic sewage by physical, biological and sometimes chemical processes to reduce solids, organic matter, nutrients and pathogens before reuse or discharge
options.C: A plant that generates electricity from waste
options.D: A plant that produces fertilizers only

questions.explanation: An STP treats domestic sewage by physical, biological and sometimes chemical processes to reduce solids, organic matter, nutrients and pathogens before reuse or discharge.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What are the main stages of conventional sewage treatment?

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is primary wastewater treatment?

options.A: Treatment that mainly removes floating and settleable solids through screening, grit removal and sedimentation
options.B: Treatment using microorganisms to break down organic matter

questions.explanation: Primary treatment mainly removes floating and settleable solids through screening, grit removal and sedimentation.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is secondary wastewater treatment?

options.A: Removal of large solids only through screening
options.B: Treatment that uses microorganisms, usually under controlled conditions, to break down dissolved and suspended biodegradable organic matter
options.C: Advanced treatment to remove nutrients and salts

questions.explanation: Secondary treatment uses microorganisms, usually under controlled conditions, to break down dissolved and suspended biodegradable organic matter.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is tertiary wastewater treatment?

options.A: Removal of large floating solids only
options.B: Additional advanced treatment used to remove remaining solids, nutrients, pathogens, salts or specific contaminants according to the intended reuse or discharge standard

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: What is the activated sludge process?

options.A: A physical method of removing large solids
options.B: A biological wastewater-treatment method in which aerated wastewater is mixed with a microbial floc, allowing microorganisms to consume organic pollutants before solids are separated
options.D: A thermal method of waste treatment

questions.explanation: The activated sludge process is a biological wastewater-treatment method in which aerated wastewater is mixed with a microbial floc, allowing microorganisms to consume organic pollutants before solids are separated.

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How can agricultural water pollution be reduced?

options.A: By applying excess fertilizers without soil testing
options.B: By applying fertilisers according to soil tests, using integrated pest management, maintaining vegetated buffer strips, preventing excessive irrigation, managing animal waste and reducing soil erosion
options.D: By removing all vegetation near water bodies

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: How can river pollution be prevented?

options.A: By discharging untreated sewage into rivers
options.B: By intercepting and treating sewage, enforcing industrial effluent standards, preventing dumping, managing solid waste, restoring riparian vegetation and monitoring water quality
options.D: By encouraging industrial discharge without treatment

questions.subject: Environmental Science
questions.question: Why should untreated sewage not be discharged into lakes and rivers?
